title: Animate Like a Pro
subtitle: Real animation with voice lessons: timing, bounce, arcs, walks and acting

lessons.title: Timing & Spacing
lessons.summary: The secret behind every animation that feels good.

steps.title: Same frames, different feel
steps.text: Both balls take 9 frames to cross. Only the spacing is different.

beats.say: Here are two balls. Both take exactly nine frames to cross the screen.
Timing is how many frames something takes. Both of these have the same timing.
Spacing is how far it moves between frames. The top ball moves the same gap every frame, so it slides like a robot.
The bottom ball starts with tiny gaps, gets fast in the middle, then tiny gaps again. That's called slow in and slow out.
Watch them again at full speed. The bottom one feels heavy and real. Pros almost always ease.

steps.title: Read a timing chart
steps.text: Animators plan spacing with a timing chart: one tick per drawing.

beats.say: This is the eased ball on its own. The dots show where it is on every frame.
Under it is a timing chart. Each tick is one drawing. Ticks close together mean slow. Ticks far apart mean fast.
Look: the ticks bunch up at both ends. That's the slow in and slow out you just saw.

steps.title: Animate a slow in and slow out
steps.text: Your project opens in Gale with 7 frames and a faint guide. On every frame, draw the ball over the guide. Small gaps at the ends, big gaps in the middle.
steps.hint: Turn on onion skin to see the last frame while you draw the next one.

quiz.question: A ball moves the same distance every frame. It will look...
quiz.explain: Even spacing has no speeding up or slowing down, so it feels stiff.

quiz.question: On a timing chart, ticks close together mean the thing is moving...
quiz.explain: Close drawings mean small moves each frame: slow.

lessons.title: The Pro Bounce
lessons.summary: Gravity, squash and stretch, all in one bounce.

steps.title: Break down a bounce
steps.text: A real bounce, worked out with gravity.

beats.say: This bounce is worked out with real gravity. Watch it a couple of times.
Falling, the ball speeds up. See how the gaps get bigger as it drops?
The faster it goes, the more it stretches. Stretch makes the speed easy to read.
On contact it squashes flat and wide. It doesn't get smaller, it just changes shape.
Going up, it slows down as gravity pulls back. Big gaps first, then small ones.
And it only bounces back to about two thirds of the height. Each bounce loses energy.

steps.title: Animate the drop
steps.text: Animate the ball falling, stretching, and squashing on the floor. Each frame, draw the ball over the guide.
steps.hint: Small gaps at the top, big gaps near the floor. Squash the last one flat.

quiz.question: Where is a falling ball stretched the most?
choices: Just before it hits the floor
quiz.explain: It's fastest right before contact, so that's where it stretches most.

quiz.question: When the ball squashes, it should...
choices: Get wider as it gets shorter
quiz.explain: Keep the same amount of ball: shorter means wider.

steps.title: A jump, pro style
steps.text: Watch what happens before and after the jump.

beats.say: Here's a little bean doing a jump. Watch the whole thing first.
Before jumping, it squashes down. That's anticipation. It tells the audience something is about to happen.
Then it launches, stretched tall. Going from squash to stretch makes the jump feel powerful.
In the air it follows gravity: up fast, slow at the top, down fast.
Landing, it squashes, then overshoots a little too tall, then settles. Nothing in real life stops dead.
Anticipation before, overshoot after. Add these to almost any action and it comes alive.

steps.title: Animate the key poses
steps.text: Seven key poses: stand, crouch, launch, in the air, land, overshoot, settle. Draw the bean on every frame over the guide.
steps.hint: The crouch is short and wide. The launch is tall and thin. Keep the bean the same size overall.

quiz.question: Anticipation is...
choices: A small move the opposite way before the main action
quiz.explain: Crouch before a jump, pull back before a throw.

quiz.question: Why add an overshoot when landing?
choices: So it doesn't stop dead and look stiff
quiz.explain: Weight keeps going a little, then settles back.

lessons.title: Arcs
lessons.summary: Living things move along curves, not straight lines.

steps.title: Swing on an arc
steps.text: A pendulum, timed by real physics.

beats.say: A pendulum swings on a curve called an arc. The rope keeps it the same distance from the top.
Here's its path. Almost everything in nature moves on arcs like this: arms, heads, tails, jumps.
It's slow at each end and fast at the bottom. Gravity gives it slow in and slow out for free.

steps.title: Straight looks wrong
steps.text: The same timing, moving in a straight line.

beats.say: Now the same spacing, but in a straight line. It looks like a machine, not a swing.
When an animation looks stiff, check the arcs. Turn on onion skin and look at the path.

steps.title: Animate the swing
steps.text: Draw the ball on every frame along the arc. Slow at the ends, fast at the bottom.
steps.hint: Follow the faint curve. Check the path with onion skin.

quiz.question: A character's hand waves hello. Its path should be...
quiz.explain: Joints turn, so the hand moves on an arc.

lessons.title: Overlapping Action
lessons.summary: Loose parts drag, then catch up.

steps.title: The tail drags behind
steps.text: A head moves and stops. The ponytail is worked out like a swinging spring.

beats.say: A head slides over and stops. Watch the ponytail.
While the head moves, the hair drags behind. It's attached at the root, but the tip is loose.
When the head stops, the hair keeps going. It swings past, swings back, then settles.
Different parts stop at different times. That's overlapping action, and it makes things feel real.

steps.title: Animate the drag and settle
steps.text: Six key frames: start, moving, stop, swing past, swing back, rest. Draw the head and ponytail on every frame.
steps.hint: The tip of the ponytail moves the most and stops last.

quiz.question: A dog runs and stops. Its ears...
choices: Stop at the exact same time
quiz.explain: Loose parts carry on, then catch up.

lessons.title: Walk Cycle
lessons.summary: The four poses that make every walk.

steps.title: The four poses
steps.text: One step has four key poses. The leg angles are worked out like a real gait.

beats.say: This is a walk cycle: two steps that loop forever.
Contact. The front heel touches down, legs spread wide.
Down. The front knee bends to catch the weight. This is the lowest point.
Passing. One leg swings past the other.
Up. The back foot pushes off and the body rises to its highest point.
Watch the head. It bobs down and up twice per cycle, once for each step.
The arms swing opposite to the legs. Right leg forward means left arm forward.

steps.title: Full speed
steps.text: Twelve frames at twelve frames per second: about one second per cycle.

beats.say: At full speed it's twelve drawings a second. The highlighted legs and arms are the near side.
The last frame leads straight back into the first, so it loops with no jump.

steps.title: Animate a walk cycle
steps.text: Eight frames, two steps. Draw the figure on every frame: body and head first, then legs, then arms.
steps.hint: Use onion skin. Each frame only changes a little from the one before.

quiz.question: When is the body lowest in a walk?
choices: The down pose, just after contact
quiz.explain: The knee bends to catch the weight, so the body dips.

quiz.question: When the right leg swings forward, the right arm swings...
quiz.explain: Arms swing opposite to the legs for balance.

steps.title: Say "Hi Mom"
steps.text: Listen for the main sounds, then pick a mouth for each.

beats.say: Let's make this face say: Hi Mom.
Say it slowly yourself. Hi is two sounds: ah, then ee.
The A mouth is wide open for ah. The E mouth is wide and flat for ee.
Mom starts with M, so the lips press shut. Then an O shape. Then shut again for the last M.
Vowels get held longer than the quick sounds. Don't animate every letter, just what you hear.
Pro tip: put the mouth one or two frames before the sound. It looks more in sync that way.

steps.title: Animate "Hi Mom"
steps.text: Draw the mouth on every frame over the guide: rest, A, E, rest, M, O, M, rest. Gale already set the holds, so press play to see it talk.
steps.hint: M, B and P are lips pressed together. O is round.

quiz.question: Which mouth shape do the M sounds in "Mom" use?
quiz.explain: M, B and P all start with the lips shut.

quiz.question: Should the mouth change for every single letter?
choices: No, just the sounds you hear

lessons.title: Face & Expression
lessons.summary: Brows, eyes and mouth tell the feeling.

steps.title: Read a face
steps.text: Five feelings on the same face. Only the brows, eyes and mouth change.

beats.say: Same face, five feelings. Only three things change: brows, eyes and mouth.
Happy. The mouth curves up and the eyes squint a little, pushed up by the cheeks.
Surprised. Brows shoot up, eyes open wide, mouth drops open.
Sad. The inner ends of the brows go up, and the mouth curves down.
Angry. The inner ends of the brows push down toward the nose.
The brows do most of the acting. Try covering the mouth: you can still tell the feeling.

steps.title: Animate a change of feeling
steps.text: Happy, then something surprises them, then they feel sad. Draw the brows, eyes and mouth on every frame.
steps.hint: Start with the brows. They show the feeling fastest.

quiz.question: Which part of the face shows feelings the most?
quiz.explain: Brows move a lot and are easy to read.

quiz.question: In a sad face, the inner ends of the brows go...
quiz.explain: Inner ends down is angry; inner ends up is sad.
